items.meta_description: Beliefs in conspiracy theories and their resistance to correction pose critical challenges to public health. A potential countermeasure to this is the use of Large Language Model (LLM) driven debates about conspiracy theories. Yet while this approach yields promising results for general conspiracies
passages: As Costello et al. rely on a randomly recruited general population sample and allow for any self-selected conspiracy to be discussed11, it seems unlikely that their participants debated deeply self-relevant conspiracy beliefs with the chatbot.
To test these assumptions, we invited participants to debate a COVID-19-related conspiracy with a chatbot labelled as either human or AI.
In an online experiment, 554 participants were randomly assigned to either a control condition or to debate an individual COVID-19 conspiracy theory with an AI-labelled LLM or a human-labelled LLM.

Chatbots reduce health-related conspiracy beliefs not because of but despite being perceived as AI.
Dialogues with large language models reduce conspiracy beliefs even when the AI is perceived as human.
This study investigates whether LLM-driven debates can reduce health-related conspiracy theories in the context of COVID-19.
Thereby we further contribute to research on chatbot-driven interventions in three ways: First, by testing the impact of LLM debates on personally relevant health-related conspiracy beliefs.
Moreover, compared to conventional debunking effects in health communication (d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.25, 0.55];43, chatbot induced reduction in conspiracy beliefs can be considered substantial.

items.meta_description: Public misinformation about wind farms threatens the global transition to net-zero and a more environmentally sustainable future. This study examines whether conversations with Generative AI (GenAI) can effectively address misinformation and improve attitudes and beliefs about wind farms. In two pre
passages: In two pre-registered experiments (collective N = 2405), participants with anti-wind farm beliefs engaged in three-round dialogues with ChatGPT, a widely used GenAI tool.
On one hand, GenAI tools such as ChatGPT have unique capabilities that make them particularly well-suited for addressing misinformation and conspiracy theories about wind farms.

Third, using ChatGPT enabled direct comparison with Costello et al.‘s30 findings, allowing us to address two questions: (1) whether the large and durable effects of AI conversations would generalise to wind farm beliefs, and (2) whether ChatGPT would remain effective without explicit persuasion instructions.
Evaluating generative AI’s potential to dispel misinformation about wind farms.
This study examines whether conversations with Generative AI (GenAI) can effectively address misinformation and improve attitudes and beliefs about wind farms.

However, as the scale and speed of wind-energy developments has ramped up in recent years, it has become apparent that negative sentiment about wind farms has expanded beyond legitimate, local concerns to incorporate misinformation and conspiracy theories circulated among the general public.
In Study 1, participants who interacted with the AI about wind farms displayed reduced agreement with misinformation immediately following the conversation (p< 0.001, 95% CI [0.11, 0.24], d = 0.44).

Furthermore, following GenAI conversations, participants displayed reduced agreement with misinformation about wind farms, increased policy support, and reduced confidence in their anti-wind farm views.
Interestingly, there is only weak evidence that people who believe misinformation about wind farms are poorly educated or lack objective scientific knowledge9.

For example, political conservatives were more likely to agree with statements about wind farms grounded in misinformation while people with pro-ecological worldviews were less likely to agree with them9.
